title: Officers and directors paid as outside contractors
question: Do the five biggest contractors on a City-funded nonprofit’s tax return include its own officers, directors, former executives or their companies?
finding: 24 top-contractor listings point back toward the organization itself: 14 where the contractor carries the full name of someone the same return lists as an officer, director or key employee (or is registered to one), the rest sharing an uncommon surname or the organization’s own address. In 8 of the 14 the person is listed with no pay and the payment is not found on the insider-transactions schedule, so the contractor line is the only place it shows; the largest is Sunny Schwartz at Five Keys Schools And Programs ($207,262).
how: Each contractor on Form 990 Part VII-B is compared with every officer, director and key employee the same organization lists in any year: the same full name; an uncommon surname inside the company name; a Treasurer business registration naming an officer as the contractor’s owner; or the contractor’s address being the organization’s own. The return is then checked for the same person’s pay in those years and Schedule L is searched for the name.
limits: Much of this is ordinary: interim chief executives and finance chiefs are often engaged as consultants, and a departing executive may be kept on contract through a handover. For a board member’s firm, the question is whether the board approved it at a fair price and the return disclosed it; “not found on Schedule L” can also mean it was reported as pay, fell below the reporting line or sits under another name. Surname-only rows may be coincidence. This goes beyond the yes/no insider answers already shown on each organization’s page.
